extracted.intended_audience: readers/scholars of early-modern natural philosophy, historical engineers, Latinists
extracted.subtask_description: A passage from an early-modern (Latin) treatise on the elements, chiefly treating the nature, generation, propagation, and technical uses of fire and smoke, with practical instructions for combustible mixtures and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of flame (flamma as heated air)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eft enim fláma nihil aliud quà aer accéfus. — Flamma nihil aliud quàm aer accessus (the flame is nothing other than air set on fire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flame is extremely subtle and perpetually moved; it does not remain identical but continually generates and succeeds into other parts. It penetrates thin parts of its subject and by its motion divides and alters subjacent substance. (Textual remarks: 'perpetuo mouet', 'tenuiffima', 'peran quitiffima', flame 'generatiene altera alteri succedit').

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of smoke
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct kinds of smoke: a thin, necessary smoke that does not suffocate or injure the eyes, and a more humid, suffocating smoke that precedes or accompanies poor/humid fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin smoke is 'necessarius' and passes through air quickly, neither suffocating nor scorching eyes, but only heats and dries. The other kind ('qui fláme preit generationé') is humid, injures the eyes, suffocates, and is common when bad or humid woods are burned ('plerüq; excarbonib? prauis àc humidiorib? lignis excitati folet').

rubrics_metrics.name: Three necessities for fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignis (fire) requires three necessities: pabulum (fuel), motus (motion), and 'quod penetrer' (that which penetrates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage states explicitly that for fire there are three necessary things: fuel, motion, and penetrating power; these are treated as jointly required for active burning and for flame to be vigorous and to enter materials ('vt ignis vrat tria (int neceffaria pabuli, motus, & quód penetrer').

rubrics_metrics.name: Flame persistence depends on available aliment
rubrics_metrics.description: A flame remains while aliment (fuel) is present; when aliment is consumed or removed, the flame ceases either spontaneously or by interruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the aliment ceases, the flame is extinguished 'sponte vel momento penitus exiringuit'. A candle's flame persists only while it has aliment; when the fuel is exhausted the flame dies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and motion affect extinguishability
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller flames are easier to extinguish; larger flames are harder to extinguish because magnitude and motion increase penetrative power and make extinguishing more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly notes that 'paruam flammá facile eft extinguere, magna autem difficillimim' and ties difficulty to the flame's motion/impetus. Hence size and the velocity of its motion (or available driving force) are key criteria for a flame's resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water extinguishes fire by multiple causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Water extinguishes fire for several reasons (threefold): it obstructs respiration/motion, it cools, and it can immerse the burning material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author says 'Ab aqua igitur vriplici ratione extinguitur' and elsewhere gives reasons: prevents air/respiration, impedes motion, and cools or submerges the burning matter; hence water's extinguishing efficacy is multifactorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and preparation of combustible powders determine behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature, ratio, and treatment of combustible powders (pyrius pulver, halinitrum, carbonis falignei, sulphur, etc.) dictate ignition ease, flame magnitude, duration, sound, and risk to machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical ratios and preparation rules are given: for great machines 'halinitri & falignei carbonis & sulphuris' in certain parts; for medium machines different proportions (e.g., 'magnis machinis... halinitri partes... sulpher duæ'), drying, sieving, washing in well water, adding vinegar, repeated drying in sun, and mixing with the finest powder are recommended. The text stresses that composition, fineness, dryness, and homogeneity control whether powder burns violently, with crepitus, or weakly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated modes of ignition/generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire may be generated by propagation, antiphysis/coition (concentration), percussion, friction, putrefaction, and coition (bringing together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage lists: 'propagatione, antifpafi, percuffione; frictione; putredine; coitione' as ways fire can arise and discusses how concentration or gathering of dispersed heat into a small space (coition) produces ignition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire is an accident (not a primary element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignis is not a substance/element but an accident: 'ignis omnino est, atque caloritas cum siccitate summa' — i.e., fire is the concurrence of great heat with dryness, an accidental state, not a separate element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues philosophically that fire depends on calor and dryness and thus is not a self-subsisting element; this is used to explain why fire appears in different materials and why it can be generated or extinguished under varying conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some substances resist fire due to impenetrability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain substances (e.g., gold and adamant) are not consumed or burned by fire because they are not penetrable by it ('aurum & adamas, ab igne non abfumuntur neque uruntur').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penetrability and subtlety determine whether fire affects a material; dense, unpenetrable bodies resist the action of flame and so remain unconsumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoke and flame motion depend on wind, vents, and chimney geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Smoke rises by impetus and lightness, but winds and the shape/number/location of openings in a hearth or chimney can repel or divert smoke; appropriate ventilation geometry reduces smoke problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text details that wind may repel smoke, narrow chimneys impede smoke exit, and that chimneys with openings on four sides (or channels) assist removal. It recommends circumferential vega (vagina) or particular canal shapes; also notes that latitude and external channels influence smoke behavior ('Venti quoq; repellunt fumü, & angustia camini prohibent').

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to preserve or rekindle fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal ways keep fire alive: by the flame's own motion (as in candles), by an external motion (bellows/folles), or by being covered/protected (e.g., under ashes or embers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author gives practical advice: keep embers under ash to prevent air access, use bellows to supply motion, or arrange fuels ('prunas') so that embers remain hot and can revive the flame; also notes that covering with ash protects from air and that minor motion can preserve small embers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration (coition) of dispersed heat produces ignition
rubrics_metrics.description: When heat that is dispersed over a large space is contracted into one small space (coition), what was mild heat becomes intense and produces ignition; this is the 'propagatione' to 'coitionem' explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage explains that gathering a quantity of heat into a smaller volume leads to larger effects ('si calor, qui per magnum spatium dispersus est, in unum contrahatur... magnus calor in parvo spatio contentus, magnos effectus producet'). Coition is offered as an important mechanism of ignition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion is the cause of heat (and thus of fire)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues (engaging Aristotelian debate) that motion causes heat; if motion is the cause of heat, then increasing motion increases heat and thus leads to ignition: 'si motus est causa caloris... Ignis autem... nihil aliud est quam calor...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise uses this principle to relate mechanical actions (friction, percussion, rapid transit of air) to the production of heat and thereby to ignition, and to explain differences among fires (some hotter and more penetrating because they are associated with greater motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for powder-driven machines (canals, spheres, weights)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using powder in machines (sphærulae, canals), dimensions and proportions matter: the canal's dimensions must match the sphere/powder, the sphere's weight should be scaled to machine power, and machine thickness and massing have specified lower bounds for safety and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules: canal diameter should correspond to the sphere size; machine bed and labrum thickness should be a significant fraction (e.g., at least a third) of the sphere's dimension; powder mass relative to sphere weight must be tuned ('pulueris podus paudlo minus esse quám sphaerulze'); avoid extremes (too fine powder may shatter machine; too coarse fails to combust uniformly). The author provides experimental proportions and cautions about fracture and channeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and handling of powder to avoid premature ignition or weak effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Powder must be thoroughly cleaned, dried, and reduced to fine particles; impurities or moisture lead to weak burning, while excessively fine or improperly confined powder can shatter machines or produce dangerous brisures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include washing in well water, drying repeatedly in sun ('in Sole siccetur'), beating with wooden mallets while submerged, adding vinegar or acetum for certain recipes, and preventing contact with damp earth. Also admonitions about not overfilling channels and ensuring reliable exits to prevent catastrophic pressure buildup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acoustic and dynamic effects of powder combustion depend on confinement and fineness
rubrics_metrics.description: If powder is confined and then suddenly freed, the violent expulsion produces sound, shock, and strong thrust; if powder burns loosely, sound and effect are weaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that a small volume of fine powder, when rapidly driven by a machine, can occupy many times the space and produce violent expulsion and loud noise; conversely, poorly elaborated or impure powder burns weakly and quietly. This informs safe design and expectations of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of fire with ice (opposite properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire and ice are contraries: fire is hot, subtle, quick, penetrating and short-lived (unless sustained), whereas ice is very cold, dense, slow, quiet, and very durable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage compares properties to explain why heat penetrates and corrupts some materials while ice resists; this is used to argue about the nature of fire and why some bodies remain unchanged by flame while others are consumed.
